text: In the game of twenty questions, a good player does not guess wildly; each question is chosen to cut the remaining possibilities roughly in half. A decision tree classifies data the same way. It asks a question about one feature, such as whether the income is above some threshold, follows the yes or no branch, asks another question, and keeps going until it reaches a leaf that announces an answer.

Each question compares a single feature with a single number, so geometrically it is a straight cut parallel to an axis. The first cut splits the plane in two, each later cut splits one of those pieces again, and the finished tree divides the plane into rectangles, each painted with the label it predicts. That makes trees easy to read: you can follow any prediction back through the exact questions that produced it.

How does the tree choose its questions? It looks for the cut that makes each side as pure as possible, meaning dominated by one class. A common measure of impurity is the Gini impurity: one minus the sum of the squared class proportions. A basket of only apples scores zero; a basket that is half apples and half oranges scores one half. For each candidate cut, we average the impurity of the two sides, weighted by how many points each holds, and keep the cut that lowers it the most.

The tree is built greedily, one question at a time. It finds the best first cut, then treats each side as a new, smaller problem and repeats, never going back to reconsider an earlier choice. Building stops when a region is pure, when it holds too few points to split sensibly, or when the tree reaches a depth limit we set in advance.

Left unchecked, a tree keeps cutting until every training point sits in its own tiny rectangle, which is memorisation, and the boundary becomes a staircase that chases every noisy point. So depth limits, a minimum number of points per leaf, and pruning back weak branches afterwards are the tree's form of regularisation, again chosen by checking a validation set.

A single tree is unstable, since a small change in the data can change the first question and everything below it. The fix is to grow many trees and combine them. A random forest trains each tree on a random resample of the data, with random subsets of features, and averages their votes, so the individual quirks cancel out. Gradient boosting instead adds trees one after another, each one trained to correct the errors left by the ones before. On tables of business data, these ensembles are still among the strongest methods available.

Language models do not use decision trees, but a related idea of routing appears inside some of them. In a mixture of experts model, a small learned router looks at each token and sends it to only a few of many expert sub-networks, a soft and trainable cousin of a tree's branching question. Next, we leave labels behind entirely and find groups with k means clustering.
